summary: One listing, one Run, and a machine that arrives and never answers. The provider allocates the capacity in twenty-four seconds and the host reaches a usable operating system three minutes later, and the node agent on it never opens a session: an image with no agent baked in, a startup script that ran before the network was up, an outbound path something is blocking. Mercator has no session to that machine, so nothing can create a container there and no workload ever begins. The record has to say so: this Run's start is unobserved and its application has said nothing, because a start is a moment somebody observed and nobody was ever able to look. That is the failure a real provider bills for, which is why the listing states both ends of it, Mercator's own ten minutes of patience and the provider's own half-hour backstop that destroys the machine whatever the control plane does. Today the corpus cannot describe this at all: every provisioned machine in both simulated worlds is assumed to be executable the moment it has booted, so the whole of enrolment is a stage that costs seconds and cannot fail.
